analysis.one_liner: Bans data brokers from collecting, selling, or keeping personal data on anyone under 18.
analysis.headline: Rep. Pallone introduced the bill with no cosponsors; a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee advanced it by voice vote on December 11, 2025, and it now awaits full committee action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for data brokers—companies that buy and resell personal information about people they never met—to collect, use, or sell personal data on anyone they know is under 18. Brokers would have to delete the data they already hold, set up a way for teens and parents to demand deletion within 10 days, and explain the process in plain language on their websites. The Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and individual families could all enforce the rules, with at least $1,000 in damages per violation and up to triple that for intentional violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers under 18, and their parents, whose personal information would no longer be collected and resold by data brokers. Families would gain a direct right to sue brokers who break the rules, with minimum damages of $1,000 per violation that cannot be waived by terms of service or forced into arbitration.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits data brokers from collecting, using, maintaining, or selling any personal data of an individual the broker knows is a child (under 13) or teen (13 to 17), and requires brokers to delete data they already hold [S2].
Requires brokers to let a teen, a parent of a child, or their agent request deletion, act on the request within 10 days, confirm completion, and publish a plain-language notice of the process [S2].

Gives families a private right of action with at least $1,000 per violation, up to triple damages for willful violations, attorney's fees, and a ban on waiving these rights through terms of service or pre-dispute arbitration agreements [S2].
Allows the FTC to enforce violations as unfair or deceptive practices, and lets state attorneys general sue on behalf of residents for injunctions, damages, and restitution [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and the advertising businesses that buy their data would lose a market: the ability to track, profile, and resell information about minors. Companies that profit from targeted ads aimed at young people would bear compliance and deletion costs.

drawbacks.text: The ban applies only to data on minors the broker 'knows' is a child or teen, defined as actual knowledge or knowledge implied by objective circumstances—so a broker can keep and sell a minor's data as long as it avoids learning the subject's age, a significant gap in coverage [S2].

Broad exceptions remove much of the market from the bill: entities acting as service providers, companies whose product is not the personal data itself, and news publishers are excluded from the definition of data broker [S2].

A minimum of $1,000 in statutory damages per violation plus mandatory attorney's fees could generate high-volume litigation against companies, a cost that critics of such provisions argue gets passed to consumers; supporters would counter that the fee-shifting is what makes enforcement real for families without resources [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: it would shut down a market where brokers profile and resell children's data, and the private right of action with unwaivable minimum damages gives families genuine leverage. The main weakness is the knowledge standard, which lets brokers escape the rules by not asking the subject's age, and the carve-outs that exempt large categories of companies. The bill is a meaningful but incomplete shield rather than a full ban on trading minors' data.

outcome.mechanism: The bill is still alive: it cleared a subcommittee of the House Energy and Commerce Committee by voice vote in December 2025 and is waiting for the full committee to act, with no floor vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill in the House on November 25, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1].
No other member had signed on as a cosponsor as of the latest record [S3].

The House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade held a markup session on December 11, 2025, and forwarded the bill to the full committee in the nature of a substitute (amended) by voice vote [S4].
No further action has been taken by the full committee, and the bill has not received a floor vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, data brokers, who can continue collecting and selling minors' data while the bill waits in committee.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes have been taken and the bill has zero cosponsors, so its support beyond the Democratic sponsor is unknown; passage would depend on the Republican-controlled committee and House bringing it up.

industries.note: These companies buy and resell personal data on people who never dealt with them directly, including minors, and the bill would outlaw collecting, holding, or selling data on anyone under 18 they know about. Their revenue depends on continuing this trade, which runs directly against the privacy of children and their families.

Advertisers and targeting firms buy broker data to aim ads at young users; losing minors' profiles shrinks the audiences they can sell to. Consumers would see fewer ads built from tracked data about their children.

industries.industry: Websites and apps that collect minors' data
industries.note: Companies acting as service providers processing data at a person's direction, or whose product is not the data itself, are excluded from the definition of data broker, so many consumer-facing platforms escape the ban while the compliance burden falls on brokers. Companies that would have been exempt gain a competitive edge over brokers subject to the rules.

analysis.trajectory: The bill advanced out of subcommittee by voice vote but has no cosponsors and no full committee or floor action scheduled. First-term bills on data brokers that clear subcommittee rarely reach the floor without broader backing; unless the full Energy and Commerce Committee marks it up and leadership schedules it, the bill is likely to remain stalled in committee for the rest of this Congress.
